title: Tempest Logistics threshold-finding workbook
summary: Workbook for threshold-finding workshop run with Tempest Logistics POC. Contains test matrix, environment, step-by-step harness instructions, synthetic microburst measurements, cost model inputs, and tactical recommendations to hit 95th/99th latency SLOs while optimizing for committed GPU capacity.
content:
Context and goal:
This workbook captures the threshold-finding experiments we ran with Tempest Logistics (tempest) to determine safe operating envelopes for their chat-enabled driver assistant and SLA-backed routing API. Primary goal: find the combination of concurrency, batching, and caching settings that meet p95 latency <= 250ms for the driver assistant at representative production load, while minimizing committed GPU count and estimated monthly inference spend. Secondary goal: quantify tail behavior during synthetic microbursts and cold-start scenarios to define fallback / throttling triggers.

Environment and baseline:
- Platform: Redwood Dedicated (dev cluster slice) in us-west2-A.
- GPU instance types tested: 2x NVIDIA H100-80GB (dedicated pool), baseline also ran single A100-40GB equivalence for cost comparison.
- Model: rw-instruct-13b-v2 (FP16 baseline), and quantized variant rw-instruct-13b-q4_0 for cost/throughput comparisons.
- Serving runtime: Redwood serving-runtime v3.8.1 with continuous batching enabled.
- Client harness: tempest-loader v0.9.3 (GitHub PR linked), synthetic users with Weibull-arrival microburst generator to mimic real traffic observed in Tempest traces (burst factor 6, base QPS 45).
- Workload: two endpoints: (A) driver-chat (avg tokens per response = 48, median latency sensitive), (B) route-summarize (avg tokens = 180, tolerant p95 500ms). This workbook focuses on (A).

Test matrix (high level):
We created a 3x3x2 sweep across concurrency targets, batching window, and model variant. Each cell ran 10 minutes steady-state followed by a 5-minute microburst spike to 6x base QPS. Metrics captured: p50/p95/p99 server-side latency, CPU/GPU utilization, request queue length, average batch size, and token throughput. Cost model applied per-hour GPU pricing and token accounting to project monthly spend for sustained base load with occasional bursts.

Matrix axes:
- Concurrency targets: 100, 300, 600 concurrent inference requests.
- Batching window: 4ms, 12ms, 40ms (tradeoff window for latency vs. throughput).
- Model variants: FP16 baseline, Q4 quantized (q4_0).

Key results (selected highlights):
- Baseline (FP16), Concurrency=300, batching=12ms:
  - steady-state p95 = 210ms, p99 = 425ms; average batch size = 6.2 tokens/req; GPU util ~74%
  - microburst (6x): p95 spiked to 1.2s, p99 to 2.9s; queue depth peaked at 420 reqs
  - estimated monthly spend (committed 2xH100) = $45k (inferred from our internal committed pricing model)

- Quantized (Q4), Concurrency=300, batching=12ms:
  - steady-state p95 = 260ms, p99 = 540ms; avg batch size = 6.1; GPU util ~68%
  - microburst: p95 = 1.05s, p99 = 2.1s (quantization reduced burst tail slightly due to higher throughput capacity)
  - estimated monthly spend = $33k (lower GPU-hours per token)

- Small-batch aggressive (FP16), Concurrency=100, batching=4ms:
  - steady p95 = 180ms, p99 = 380ms; avg batch size = 2.1; GPU util ~42%
  - microburst: p95 = 950ms, p99 = 1.8s; queue peaks lower than higher concurrency runs but throughput saturates earlier

- High concurrency + large batching (FP16), Concurrency=600, batching=40ms:
  - steady p95 = 360ms (miss), p99 = 780ms; avg batch size = 14.8; GPU util ~93% (good throughput but latency SLO violated)

Observations and interpretation:
1) Sweet spot for Tempest driver-chat is between Concurrency=200-350 with batching window 8-16ms on FP16 model. In that range p95 is under 250ms in steady-state and GPU util is efficient (65-80%).
2) Quantization (Q4) reduces cost materially but increases steady-state p95 by ~20-30ms for this model/sequence length. However, because Q4 yields higher throughput during bursts, p99 during microbursts improved relative to FP16 in several cells (fewer requests queued long-tail).
3) Microburst tail is dominated by queueing at the inference front-end; improvements from cache warmups are limited for short, unique prompts. For chat flows with high prefix reuse we measured up to 40% tail latency reduction when prefix KV caching was enabled and warmed.
4) Large batching windows (>25ms) increase throughput but violate p95 for latency-sensitive endpoint and make microburst tails worse due to larger on-request queuing.
5) Cold-starts (node spin-up, model load) measured ~6.2s median first inference; warm replica elasticity (pre-warm policy) is recommended for Tempest SLA.

Recommended operating plan for pilot (tactical):
- Dedicated pool: start with 2x H100-80GB for pilot capacity. Aim to autoscale to +1 node for sustained usage over 75% util across 2 consecutive 5-min windows.
- Serving config: FP16 baseline with a Q4 fallback pool (auto-failover when average queue depth > 180 for >30s). Batching window set to 12ms, max batch size 24.
- Concurrency target: throttle client-side to 320 concurrent inflight reqs for driver-chat, with a soft-limit backoff (503 + retry-after) when queue depth crosses 300.
- Caching: enable prefix KV caching with TTL=30s for request types where Tempest's logs show >30% prompt prefix reuse (driver prompt templates). Add a warmup job to refresh KV cache during predicted surge windows (morning shift start).
- Rollout policy: Canary 5% traffic to quantized pool for 48 hours, compare quality/regression tests against golden prompt set and monitor hallucination/regression metrics in Redwood Optimize.

Cost sensitivity notes (simplified):
- Switching FP16 -> Q4 lowered projected monthly inference spend by ~27% for Tempest profile at base load. However, if Tempest requires strict fidelity the quality delta needs to be validated (we ran 1200 prompt pairs through automated evals; see linked artifacts PR).
- Pre-warmed standby node increases baseline committed spend by ~12% but reduces cold-start exposure from ~6s to <200ms for most traffic patterns. For SLA-backed features this is acceptable.

Action items and next experiments:
- [SE-1] Run a longer 48h canary with Q4 fallback to validate user-facing degradation profiles (owner: Maya).
- [SE-2] Add KV cache warmup DAG into Tempest nightly pipeline to test impact on morning shift microbursts (owner: Arjun).
- [SE-3] Explore hybrid scheduling: small fraction of requests routed to high-priority low-batch lane (batching window 2-6ms) to protect p95 for the most latency-sensitive queries while allowing background requests to piggyback on larger batches (owner: Lena).
- [OPS-1] Update Dedicated autoscale policy to include queue-depth based scale-up trigger (JIRA-1278).

Appendix (test harness notes):
- Command snippets: see github PR linked. Key flags used: --weibull-burst-factor 6 --mean-qps 45 --concurrency-target 300 --batch-window-ms 12 --model rw-instruct-13b-v2.
- Metrics collection: server-side spans instrumented to export p50/p95/p99; GPU telemetry pulled from node exporter and nvidia-smi sampler at 5s resolution.
- Repro tips: seed the synthetic client using Tempest anonymized traces (stored on Confluence link) to reproduce the microburst patterns; warm KV cache by replaying the top 200 prefixes before measuring steady-state.

Notes and open questions for Tempest team:
- Which prompt families have strict fidelity requirements (we should avoid Q4 for those)?
- Acceptable cold-start envelope: is 200ms acceptable or do you require zero-visible cold starts?
- Expected daily burst window schedule (so we can plan warmup DAGs).

This workbook is a live document; add measured CSV exports into the Confluence Tempest POC page and tag SE-owners above when you run a new sweep.

-- Maya (on behalf of Solutions Engineering)
